EntertainmentTab.title: Dolly Parton's manager accuses nephew who announced her death of threats and intimidation
EntertainmentTab.text:
Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's legacy and business interests.

The accusations against Bryan Seaver, who was Parton's head of security and was handpicked to announce her death last month, have been made public in US legal documents filed this week.

The company that manages Parton's businesses and properties, She's Alive, is seeking a temporary civil restraining order against him.

In court filings, She's Alive alleged that Seaver mounted "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", claiming he said he would ruin her empire if the estate did not pay him. He has denied the claims.

In a statement to TMZ, external, he said that text messages and emails quoted in the court application had been taken out of context to make it look like he was threatening people.

"Nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by," he said.

"A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."

Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns a company that provided the singer's security detail for the last 20 years of her life.

Last week, he was fired by She's Alive as head of security for her properties.

In a statement at the time, Seaver and his company said the dismissal was "unexpected" and "unexplained".

They added: "We refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much."

The request for a restraining order was filed in Nashville on Tuesday by She's Alive, which is run by Parton's longtime manager Danny Nozell.

The court documents quoted a series of exchanges in which someone, identified by the estate as Seaver, threatened to destroy Parton's brand.

In one, he's alleged to have said he would become "the hand of retribution for my entire family", according to the court documents.

Another said: "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or [expletive] pay me."

The papers also claimed that Seaver used his experience as a military contractor to intimidate employees.

In an exchange with one of Parton's lawyers, he allegedly described himself as a "killer" and said that on the day his aunt died, he had sold $27m (£20m) in arms and ammunition to the Haitian police.

"All I do is warfare... Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do," he was accused of saying, according to a copy of an email attached to the complaint.

In his statement published on TMZ, Seaver said: "I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer."

But he denied making threats and said he had been "talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend".

The messages have resulted in some employees and lawyers for Parton's trusts and estates resigning, according to the court documents.

She's Alive has also had to hire private security for its employees, including at their homes, the filing states.

The BBC has contacted Seaver and She's Alive for further comment.

Previously, Seaver was known to the public for announcing his aunt's death in a video posted to her Instagram account on 25 August.

Speaking in front of a black background, he was sombre and reflective as he introduced himself and shared the unexpected news.

"This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality," he said in the video.

Seaver added that he had followed in his father Larry's footsteps in becoming Parton's head of security, a post he held for more than 20 years.

Nozell started working for Parton in 2004, first as a tour consultant and later as her manager.

In the 2019 Netflix film, Dolly Parton: Here I Am, he said his job was to transform her from a "heritage act" into a "superstar", and he took responsibility for reviving her international touring career.

In a statement last month, he said the singer had "worked up until the day she died" on multiple projects, and envisioned a legacy that continued long beyond her death.

"She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy," he said in the statement.

"Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come."

The estate now faces a public tug of war over that legacy.

EntertainmentTab.title: Gavin and Stacey stars join Ruth Jones for 60th birthday party at RAFA club
EntertainmentTab.text:
Gavin and Stacey's Ruth Jones has celebrated her 60th birthday at a social club with co-stars including James Corden and Rob Brydon.

The party took place at the Porthcawl and Kenfig Hill RAFA (Royal Air Force Association) Club on Saturday where her parents were members for several years.

Corden, who co-wrote the series and played Smithy - the love interest of Jones' Nessa - helped behind the bar pouring beers, while Jones reconnected with Brydon to sing country classic Islands in the Stream on stage.

Sarah Prescott, the club's steward, described the evening as "overwhelming and unbelievable", thanking Jones for choosing the club to host the event.

The private celebration was also attended by cast members Melanie Walters and Alison Steadman, as well as Steve Speirs, a close collaborator of Jones'.

"We didn't realise how big of an event it was until the actual night when they were all coming through the door," Prescott said.

"It was quite overwhelming and unbelievable," she said, adding it had been kept private and required careful planning.

Prescott said Jones chose the venue because of its strong connection to her family, with both her parents long-standing members.

"She used to come here as a child and had her first guitar lesson at the RAFA club, so she does hold the club dearly," she said.

EntertainmentTab.title: George Bush, murder and nautical infidelity: the Chicks’ 20 greatest songs – ranked!
EntertainmentTab.text:
20. If I Fall You’re Going Down With Me (2001)

One of eight singles released from the album Fly. Amazement at the sheer number should be matched by astonishment at their consistency. If I Fall … is just great. Organ-driven rock lent a Nashville twang by the fiddle, it barrels along, rich with the confidence of a band who know they can’t put a foot wrong.

19. Tights on My Boat (2020)

You don’t want for dirt dished about Natalie Maines’ divorce on Gaslighter, the band’s eighth album, but this accusation of nautical infidelity stands out. It’s ferociously angry and very funny – plus its understated, live-in the-studio sound only compounds the sense that you’re eavesdropping on tea being spilled among friends.

18. You Were Mine (1998)

A great country weeper in its own right, You Were Mine is also part of the Chicks’ origin story. It was written by the sisters Emily Strayer and Martie Maguire about their parents’ divorce; they then invited Maines, the daughter of the producer Lloyd Maines, to sing on the demo, rather than the then Chicks vocalist Laura Lynch. A lineup change and vast success ensued.

17. The Long Way Around (2006)

The chief theme of the Taking the Long Way album – being celebrated soon with a 20th anniversary reissue and tour – was the Chicks’ war of words with President George W Bush and Nashville conservatives. The musically sweet-toned opening track suggests that attitude was par for the course – of a piece with a longstanding disinclination to “kiss all the asses” and “do it like everybody else”.

16. Julianna Calm Down (2020)

Over a soft organ backing and something approaching a dancefloor pulse, the Chicks offer hard-won advice to the recently dumped: “Put on your best shoes and strut the fuck around like you’ve got nothing to lose.” Its slow build to a euphoric climax – elevated by Maguire’s fiddle – is great.

15. Ready to Run (1999)

You could suggest the Celtic motifs on Ready to Run are an acknowledgment of Irish folk’s seminal influence on country; equally, they may have something to do with the Corrs’ late-90s success. Either way, Ready to Run’s breezy mood carries a witty lyric that offers a middle finger to marriage and commitment.

14. Texas Man (2020)

Marooned in California post-divorce, Maines pines for the more rough-hewn gents of her home county. But the beauty of Texas Man is really about the music’s experimental bent: a tight, close-miked, new-wave-leaning sound replete with fuzzed-out guitar that’s completely unlike anything the Chicks had released before, but still somehow sounds like them.

13. Cold Day in July (1999)

Five minutes of inconsolable misery. “The moon is full, and my arms are empty / All night long, I’ve pleaded and cried,” it opens, with Maines’ voice at its most angst-ridden. The guitar-driven arrangement is simple, but spot-on: it doesn’t need anything more to work its sob-inducing magic.

12. Sin Wagon (1999)

In the early 80s, there was talk of a subgenre called cowpunk. It never crossed over into the mainstream, but the title perfectly fits Sin Wagon, named after a line in Grease. A thrilling blend of speedy bluegrass with raw, growling energy, its lyrics are home to a splendid celebration of “mattress dancin”.

11. Sleep at Night (2020)

There’s a pleasing circularity about Sleep at Night, which bears the distinct influence of the noted Chicks fan Taylor Swift; you can almost hear her delivering the line: “My husband’s girlfriend’s husband just called me up – how messed up is that?” An extra point for the slapping rhythm track, the perfect accompaniment to the punches landed in the lyrics.

10. Easy Silence (2006)

The negative image of Taking the Long Way’s two-fisted lead single Not Ready to Make Nice, Easy Silence details the downside of being the centre of a media storm. It sounds utterly, affectingly weary – “everyone is running” it notes, before evincing a longing to “keep the world at bay”.

9. There’s Your Trouble (1998)

The Chicks’ biggest UK chart hit offers the perfect example of why their fourth album, Wide Open Spaces, catapulted the former bluegrass/western-swing combo to superstardom: beautifully turned songwriting, a fresh pop sheen that didn’t overwhelm their audible country bona fides, impressively tough and salty lyrics and – in their new vocalist Maines – the ideal voice to deliver them.

8. Landslide (2002)

This version of the Stevie Nicks song is bold – the original is a classic – and ahead of the curve, arriving years before Fleetwood Mac became a hip name for leftfield musicians to drop. Stripped down to country basics, in keeping with the rest of the album Home, the song shines, highlighting the trio’s impeccable harmonies.

7. Long Time Gone (2002)

The back-to-the-land saga of Darrell Scott’s Long Time Gone comes complete with a critique of modern Nashville – “they got money, but they don’t have Cash” – and the Chicks’ version is suitably old-fashioned, with no drums and a distinct bluegrass influence about the banjo and fiddle. The lyrics are biting, but it still sounds like a party.

6. Gaslighter (2020)

The title track of the first Chicks album in 14 years pulled no punches. Its subject, Natalie Maines’ ex-husband Adrian Pasdar, had reportedly been concerned that the group’s unreleased material would violate a confidentiality clause in their prenuptial agreement. Gaslighter was released after the couple finalised their divorce, but it is almost unsettlingly brutal in its frankness – and insanely catchy.

5. Wide Open Spaces (1998)

Wide Open Spaces started life as a student’s poem about returning to Texas from university in Montana and ended up a kind of Stetson-clad She’s Leaving Home. A huge hit – and the kind of Chicks song that one suspects sunk in deep with the young Swift.

4. Travelin’ Soldier (2002)

This is destined to be remembered as the track Maines was introducing in London when she criticised Bush, but the ensuing furore shouldn’t overshadow how fantastic Travelin’ Soldier is. Stark and moving, never mawkish, it isn’t a protest song so much as a heartbreaking story entwined with the Vietnam war.

3. Cowboy Take Me Away (1999)

A song based on the slogan of a US advert – for Calgon bath and beauty products! – should be a novelty. Cowboy Take Me Away is anything but. Instead, it’s a wistful paean to escape, lent a tear-jerking quality by the sense said escape may never happen. Balanced between uplift and melancholy, the music fits perfectly.

2. Not Ready to Make Nice (2006)

The Chicks’ best-known musical response to the Bush incident is a thing of snarling, screw-the-lot-of-you wonder: “It’s too late to make it right / I probably wouldn’t if I could.” The ensuing album slightly belaboured the point, but as a short, sharp burst of bitterness and bile, Not Ready to Make Nice is a triumph.

1. Goodbye Earl (1999)

Long before controversy engulfed their career, the Chicks were entirely capable of causing it. Twenty country stations refused to play Goodbye Earl, apparently horrified by the lyric: high school friends Mary-Anne and Wanda successfully plot to murder Wanda’s abusive husband after he breaches a restraining order and leaves her in intensive care. It still sold a million copies – deservedly so. The chorus is a singalong monster, the lyric is gripping and superbly written and the Chicks’ reading of it is perfect. The vocals switch from cold rage to gleeful celebration over music that is taut and explosive. Tongues firmly in cheek, they stuck a cover of Stand By Your Man on the B-side.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘I get lost going to the bathroom’: John Hannah on world travel, stealing props and being ‘the Scottish Eminem’
EntertainmentTab.text:
How often do you get asked to recite that WH Auden poem from Four Weddings and a Funeral, and can you do it from memory right now? mattyjj and simoit

Not for a long time. I could probably do the first couple of lines: Stop all the clocks, cut off the telephone / Prevent the dog from barking with a juicy bone / Turn out the lights? And with muffled drums / Something, something … let the mourners come. There you go. Terrible!

In Steve Coogan’s Paul Calf’s Video Diary, your character praises Orson Welles’ The Trial for its “tremendous energy”, while Paul says he would “rather watch Dave Lee Travis playing Macbeth”. What’s your actual opinion of The Trial [by Franz Kafka]? AdrianH1

God, it’s a long time since I’ve read that. I read a lot of those books in my younger days, but probably, like a lot of people, even those who are graduates of English literature, I’d be hard pushed these days to tell you what it was about, other than the persecution of some minor character.

As a popular jobbing actor, you have a massive list of credits. Has anyone ever come up to you to express their appreciation for a certain role and you had no idea what they were on about? Kevcoe

No. It’s always heartwarming when somebody comes up and offers their congratulations on something a little bit lower down the pecking order. Fortunately, people rarely ever come up to tell me that they thought I was shit in something. I quite often get Paul Calf’s Video Diary, and that Macbeth line. To be frank, I can’t quite remember the context.

Should Eminembe thanking you for Stan, rather than Dido, given that he first heard Thank You on the Sliding Doors soundtrack? vammyp

It’s strange how Sliding Doors and Four Weddings have travelled the world. It’s certainly cool to think that somebody as far out of left field as Eminem has actually even seen something you’ve done. Although, the story I heard was he was so sickened by the sweetness that he decided to counterpoint it with an obsessed fan trying to murder his girlfriend.

What’s your Sliding Doors moment? Murdomania

It’s interesting that “sliding doors” as an expression has become such common parlance, hasn’t it? I certainly don’t run for trains any more.

I was so traumatised by your characters in Truth or Dare and Carnivàle that whenever I see you in anything else, I think: “Oh no, it’s that horrible man.” Do you enjoy playing characters like that? FioreSebek

There you go: a prime example of something coming from left field. I do think that old cliche is true about bad guys always being more fun. I also get to play a lot of scientists or doctors, because for some reason, my Scottish accent makes me sound educated.

Which was most fun: filming Charlie Brooker’s police procedural parody A Touch of Cloth, or appearing in an episode of Black Mirror? MrMustard

A Touch of Cloth was great fun. We certainly had to do a lot of takes for all the laughing. Black Mirror felt more like a 1980s dark BBC late-night psychopath drama. Working with Charlie was quite high-concept in Black Mirror, but high camp in Cloth.

Apparently, you nicked some props from The Mummy to decorate your then-new home. What have you pinched since? Ludders

It’s like the old joke: you shag one sheep … You nick one prop. It was this fibreglass, spray-painted gold, Egyptian dog head with arms all going in different directions. I had a tiny garden at the time, and thought it would be something to look at other than a wall. But Brendan [Fraser] took the piss out of me, and constantly said I nick stuff. I can imagine Ridley Scott’s allowed to steal Aliens and put them in his vineyard. Richard E Grant’s a bit of a klepto too – he’s got shitloads in his garden. And Alan Cumming is a bit sticky-fingered.

If you took part in Celebrity Race Across the World, would you still narrate it in the third person? AngryTomato

Well, the bottom line is I wouldn’t be doing Race Across the World. I get lost going to the bathroom. I’ve missed planes, turned up on the wrong day, got off the train at the wrong stop … I’m no good at stuff. So I’d be terrible.

Have you ever had more fun on a set than on Spartacus – thundering great big lines of fruity dialogue about “Thracian whores” while lounging about in various states of distress with Lucy Lawless? mikebhoy

It was pretty spectacular. As we mentioned earlier, it’s always fun playing the villain. You only got the scripts as you were shooting, so you never knew what was coming next. Some of the stuff, you could not believe. I think in episode two, I come into our chamber with Lucy Lawless. We’re about to have a bit of how’s-your-father, but it’s been a stressful day, so she gets one of the servants to get me going by fellating me, so I had to deliver all this dialogue, while pretending to be fellated. If I had to live in Roman times, I know where I’d like to be. I’d definitely want to be upstairs.

Did the Co-op employ you to do their voiceovers because you have the perfect Scottish accent to rhyme “good” with “food”? OnTheEdgeOfEurope

No, I think that was one of those happy coincidences. I don’t think they realised that it could possibly rhyme. It’s like when Eminem rhymes all these things with “orange”. I’m the Scottish Eminem!

In Agents of SHIELD, you created Life Model Decoys of people. If you could make one of anyone in real life, who would you choose? NotCEEFAUXhonest

My dad. He died 11 years ago. My mum, too. It’s funny, you still miss them. I wish I could phone them up and tell them what was happening, what was going on. As a parent, my kids are never off their phones, but you never hear from them unless they want money. I think back to when I left home at 16 and, if I wanted to phone my parents, I’d have to grab a handful of coins and head across the street to the phone box, which I probably did once a month. Recognising how things are now as a parent, I sort of wish I’d got to know my parents better. If you asked me who I could have dinner with, alive or dead, I’d speak to my mum and dad. I’d ask them all this shit I wish I could have asked them before.

You’ve had a really diverse career, despite some people’s attempts to pigeonhole you as a Scottish mummy’s boy. What’s left on the bucket list? AmongstTheWaves

Well, when I turned 60, I joked with my kids that I was retiring. What that meant was I felt comfortable with what I’d achieved. Maybe there were sort of gaps, maybe it wasn’t quite as great a career as I would have liked, but I was going to step back from trying to have a career. I think I spent too long seeing jobs as a step to the next job, and didn’t really appreciate the moment. So turning 60 I thought: “Bollocks to this, I’m just going to do stuff that I like, that’s filming somewhere nice, or is especially well paid. If it’s got two out of three of those things, I’ll do it.”

The reality is that I’ve probably never been busier. Stuff like Bad Day at the Office comes out of left field. After decades of complaining about playing cops and being a Scottish mummy’s boy it was nice to do something that was so ridiculous, strange and experimental that, at 64, you could never have imagined it.

Do you and James Nesbitt ever go out for a pint together just to watch the confusion on people’s faces? RobinGoodfellow

We used to play five-a-side back in the 90s. The last time I bumped into him was when his daughter and my son graduated from Manchester uni, last summer. It’s good if people think I’m Jimmy Nesbitt, because I can then swear at them and be rude and he gets the blame.

When did you last use the expression “by Jupiter’s cock”? wellywearer2

This morning, funnily enough.

GeneralTab.title: Brain tumour diagnosis cut from weeks to hours with rapid new NHS test
GeneralTab.text:
A rapid new test for brain tumours that the NHS has started using can slash the time it takes for an accurate diagnosis from up to eight weeks to two hours.

The test, which is used by doctors to diagnose which type of tumour a patient has, should mean patients can start treatment including radiotherapy and chemotherapy sooner, and are spared weeks of uncertainty.

GeneralTab.title: Netanyahu defends Israeli military action as delegates walk out before UN speech
GeneralTab.text:

GeneralTab.title: New policies, election speculation: What to expect from Burnham's first Labour conference as PM
GeneralTab.text:
Andy Burnham had plenty to say about where the government - and the country - was going wrong at last year's Labour conference in Liverpool.

But that was at a fringe meeting on the sidelines of the main event.

Now, as Labour leader and prime minister, he is the main event - and it is down to him to show party members and the wider public that he has some answers.

Earlier this week, he said his debut leader's speech would leave nobody in any doubt about "what I'm trying to do in this role".

"People are going to know the direction I want to take this country and I will set it down quite clearly," he told reporters en route to the UN General Assembly in New York.

An internal No 10 note has set out the broad themes he will explore when he takes to the stage in Liverpool on Tuesday - including setting out long-term solutions to build a belief that the future can be brighter.

The slogan for this year's conference is "Hope Again".

So in his speech he is likely to point to his forthcoming 10 Year Plan for the UK – which, he says, will have "making life more affordable" at its core.

As for the specifics of what he will say, some of it will be very familiar to anyone who was listening to his conference fringe speech 12 months ago.

Back then, he declared then that the country had "lost control" of "the essentials" following the Thatcher-era sell off of utilities and that we were all "overpaying for water, housing energy, transport".

He called for a renewed emphasis on technical education and wanted to see a decade of council house building on the scale of the post-war Labour government.

For a politician frequently denounced for "flip flopping" he has been remarkably consistent in recent times.

He is likely to re-alight on themes from his Labour leadership campaign – saying more about his commitment to greater "public control" – though not necessarily public ownership - of life's necessities; building national resilience in an unstable world; and investing political capital in the reform of social care.

A potential crowd pleaser would be to tell Labour activists from the main stage what he told them as Greater Manchester mayor from the fringe last year – that he will set up a commission to examine electoral reform.

Such a move would be supported by about a quarter of his own MPs and would tie in with his leadership campaign promise of "a new politics", focused on "problem solving" rather than "point scoring".

We are also likely to hear more about getting young people into work or training, with the conclusions of the review by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn likely to be published soon.

And there is certain to be plenty about his efforts to devolve power away from Whitehall to England's mayors and the new No 10 North.

The task for Burnham is to meld these snapshots into a compelling and coherent narrative, culminating in a vision of the Britain he wants to see a decade from now.

But there are already worries that this might become a fictional narrative unless he also focuses even more on the here and now.

After all, Sir Keir Starmer's "decade of national renewal" was binned after just two bumpy years in office.

Party insiders say measures such as removing VAT from electricity bills are just the start of that assistance.

But Labour's biggest union funder, Unite, wants to see much more robust action on living costs sooner rather than later. The union does not want the promise of jam tomorrow, but some instant sweeteners.

Its leader, Sharon Graham, has called for a "winter fuel in reverse" – a policy from Burnham next week which would be as popular as Starmer's early removal of payments from many pensioners was unpopular.

The union has put forward a motion which gives the PM plenty of options such as a cap on energy prices and unfreezing tax thresholds – an issue Burnham himself said had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to be the MP for Makerfield.

The union has said revenue can be raised through a windfall tax on banks. The umbrella body for unions, the TUC, has called for an increase in the bank surcharge to subsidise energy bills.

All eyes will be on John Healey's first conference speech as chancellor on Monday.

With borrowing costs for last month soaring to their second highest level, his room for manoeuvre is limited and he will not scoop his own Budget next month by announcing what is in it.

But Labour activists will be keen to know from his language whether Healey's Treasury will opt for continuity or will represent a break from the past two years under Rachel Reeves, not just in rhetoric but reality.

Some in Labour's ranks believe Burnham is planning for an early election, with party HQ recently launching "operation second term", to beef up its campaigning and organising strength.

Burnham does not have to call an election until August 2029 - but going to the country early - perhaps as early as next spring - could deliver him a mandate of his own and free him from the constraints of Sir Keir Starmer's 2024 manifesto.

Recent polling has suggested that a "Burnham bounce" is real, though not dramatic.

The party has moved from just under 20% in the polls at the end of the Starmer era to around the mid-twenties now.

Ipsos puts its standing as high as 28%, external, while YouGov registers a more modest 23%, external.

Labour strategists will be pleased that Reform UK's share – 21% in YouGov - is the lowest since January 2025, and that Nigel Farage's party is now neck-and-neck with Kemi Badenoch's Conservatives.

One Labour insider told me that Burnham is happy to see a resilient Badenoch, as this blunts Reform support and could point to a split vote on the right at an election.

And new research from YouGov, external suggests that at the all important constituency level, 63-68% of Lib Dem and Green voters would tactically vote for Labour to stop Reform UK winning their seat.

Burnham of course also faces a challenge on the left.

How much of a threat Zack Polanski's Greens can be in some traditional Labour seats will be tested in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election just a week after the Labour conference concludes.

Downing Street insists that an early election is not being planned.

To say anything else, though, would be to repeat the uncertainty of Gordon Brown's early months in No 10 when election speculation wasn't doused - and had become so rife that he was reputationally damaged when he decided not to go to the polls.

But some who have been in regular touch with No 10 tell me they have seen no serious signs that an early election is in the offing.

Burnham appears determined to give his government enough time in office to present tangible achievements to a sceptical electorate.

And with Labour still well below the 34% vote share it captured in 2024, many Labour MPs will be pushing the PM not to cut and run.

So don't expect the centre point of Burnham's conference speech to be a message to his MPs to go back to their constituencies and prepare for a loss of some of their seats.

But equally don't expect election speculation to subside at this conference.

The Labour Party has tried and trusted methods of managing dissent at party conferences, when it comes to votes on party policy.

But the coming week could see a concerted effort by some on the left to push for a complete ban on arms sales to Israel and for Israel's actions in Gaza to be described by Labour as a genocide.

Those close to Burnham believe he has gained considerable credit by sanctioning the illegal Israeli settlements on the West Bank and won't need to go further.

There is also some frustration that his government has not yet revised proposals to make migrants wait much longer to gain permanent residency rights, and there are genuine differences over whether the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields should go ahead.

But while Burnham is facing some difficult calls, this is not a leader facing a restless party in revolt.

He has offered to give the hard-pressed public "breathing space" amid a cost of living crisis.

And his own party is so far giving him breathing space as leader – largely sighing with relief that it is not Sir Keir Starmer who will be delivering the main address this year.

Senior Labour officials have hailed the forthcoming conference as an opportunity to "show voters a party that is boldly, confidently, and authentically Labour".

But not too far below the political radar, there are already demands from some in the wider Labour movement to prove it.

GeneralTab.title: 'We're all broke': Would you chase a friend for £5?
GeneralTab.text:
You pick up the bill for dinner, pay for the taxi home or grab a friend's coffee with the promise they'll pay you back later, but days go by and the money never arrives.

At what point do you ask them for it again and how small is too small to chase?

For some, $5 (£3.70) is worth a reminder, while for others, asking a friend to repay anything under $20 (£15) feels more awkward than simply taking the hit.

Henry Payne says he's "sent a request for $8.50, but I wouldn't go lower than $8".

The 21-year-old New Yorker adds that he will chase someone once but "two requests is insane".

"I would rather swallow the $8.50 than send another request."

He does admit that he's sometimes the person on the other side of the transaction and can be forgetful himself.

"For everyone that I haven't sent back money to, I just forgot, feel free to double request me."

Kaz Jahanbini, 19, says needing to ask to be paid back in the first place can be frustrating.

"If someone bought me something, I'm immediately paying them back. So then I'm thinking for them, what's the delay?"

His rule for navigating friendship and finances is to "keep your wallet close but your friends closer".

His friend Nouria agrees and says as a student "every extra dollar counts" but she would usually only ask for money back from a friend if it was more than $10.

A recent study, external found that 76% of Gen Z who have fronted money for a group expense, like a trip or event, say they were not fully repaid, and 55% say it created tension or negatively affected a relationship.

For British student Betsie Brooke-Taylor, 19, the threshold to ask for money back is a fiver as she says "every little helps".

She sees a cultural difference between the UK and US and even though "we are all broke, I think Americans are a bit more generous".

Betsie also thinks technology makes settling small debts easier in the US, where payment apps such as Venmo are widely used.

Venmo lets users send and request money through an app which includes the function of sending a reminder if someone hasn't paid you. In the US, more than 95 million people have a Venmo account, external.

"In the UK you have to ask for the account number and sort code, and not everyone has that on hand," she says.

For 19-year-old Annika Violet, the amount she would ask back from a friend depends on whether she's consistently paying for them.

"I prefer to do something where I get them this time and they get me next time but if I'm consistently paying and you're not, then I will request the $5."

Unlike many, Annika doesn't find money conversations uncomfortable.

"I am so confrontational, I do not find it awkward. If you're my friend, you would pay me back."

Annika's friend Hanako Stepper says she finds it awkward asking for money but wishes she didn't.

"I've never chased anyone - I'm just sad if I don't get paid back."

Annika's advice to those who do struggle to ask is to "be brave and bold".

"If they are going to give you flak about it, maybe it's a sign they are not a good friend."

Several people the BBC spoke to said the amount itself mattered less when somebody repeatedly failed to pay.

New York student Ella Feuille, 21, says $15 is roughly the point at which she would consider requesting money.

If a significant amount was owed, Ella says she would ask around three times before giving up but wouldn't necessarily forget about it.

"I have friends who I know now it has to go on their card because they're not going to pay me back."

Her friend Katrina Dimingot agrees and says she much prefers a method where "we don't pay each other back, we just take it in turns to get things for each other".

GeneralTab.title: Reported assaults on Britain's rail services rise by more than a third
GeneralTab.text:
Reports of violent incidents and harassment on rail services "rose substantially" last year, figures from the rail regulator show.

Reported assaults, including physical and verbal, were up 36% in the year to March 2026 compared with the previous year, according to the Office of Rail and Road (ORR).

In total 13,464 assaults against passengers and members of the public were recorded on Britain's mainline railway, the highest number recorded since the series began in 2004.

The ORR said the figures were "concerning" and that it was working with the industry to address the problem.

According to the figures, harassment increased by 52% compared with the previous year and common assaults rose by 30%.

The increase comes against a backdrop of five years of rising reports of incidents and industry campaigns to raise awareness.

Assaults on the mainline railway are recorded according to their type. As a result each incident can lead to reports in more than one category, for example if someone is harassed and then physically assaulted.

There were also 11,289 reported assaults against members of the workforce on the mainline railway, up 12% compared with the previous year.

Of those 2,487 were physical assaults, while more than half (6,390 incidents) involved verbal abuse. The rest were threats.

"We're working with industry and our trade union colleagues to address work-related violence and harassment," said Richard Hines, the ORR's chief inspector of railways.

"This includes understanding where the risks are, putting effective controls in place, encouraging staff to report incidents and providing appropriate support afterwards," he said.

The statistics include mainline rail services in England, Scotland and Wales, but not Northern Ireland. The data release also covers the London Underground, trams, metros and other light rail services.

On the London Underground, recorded assaults increased 20% to 5,534 in the latest year, but reported workforce assaults fell 3% to 3,525.

Transport for London does not record multiple aspects of each incident. Instead it records the most severe aspect reported.

A spokesperson responding on behalf of Network Rail and the train companies said all operators were working to reduce risk and prevent harm by sharing information, improving reporting processes and deploying body-worn cameras.

"Keeping passengers and colleagues safe is at the heart of everything we do," the spokesperson said.

"Violence, abuse and intimidation directed at passengers or staff are completely unacceptable. The rail industry works closely with British Transport Police to investigate incidents, support victims and bring offenders to justice."

The passenger body, Transport Focus, said the ORR's figures supported research it conducted which found personal security was "one of the highest priorities" for passengers. However, only 3% of passengers it surveyed said they were dissatisfied with personal safety at the station.

Transport Focus acknowledged that some of the increase might reflect better reporting. Nevertheless, every incident represented someone negatively affected, it said, adding it would like to see "a much more strategic approach" to tackling the issue.

The RMT union, representing rail industry workers, said the figures corresponded with the union's own figures indicating two-thirds of its members had experienced violence at work.

RMT general secretary Eddie Dempsey called for an increase in staffing on public transport, including an end to lone working, to combat the problem.

"We also clearly need stronger legal protections for public transport workers against assaults at work," he said.

He said cuts to British Transport Police funding had been "disastrous" and called for outsourced security and enforcement staff to be brought in-house "as a matter of urgency".

Other notable figures from the statistical release include that 11 members of the public died at mainline level crossings in the latest year, six more than the previous year. Eight were pedestrians and the others were road vehicle users.

He is likely to re-alight on themes from his Labour leadership campaign – saying more about his commitment to greater "public control" – though not necessarily public ownership - of life's necessities; building national resilience in an unstable world; and investing political capital in the reform of social care.

A potential crowd pleaser would be to tell Labour activists from the main stage what he told them as Greater Manchester mayor from the fringe last year – that he will set up a commission to examine electoral reform.

Such a move would be supported by about a quarter of his own MPs and would tie in with his leadership campaign promise of "a new politics", focused on "problem solving" rather than "point scoring".

We are also likely to hear more about getting young people into work or training, with the conclusions of the review by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn likely to be published soon.

And there is certain to be plenty about his efforts to devolve power away from Whitehall to England's mayors and the new No 10 North.

The task for Burnham is to meld these snapshots into a compelling and coherent narrative, culminating in a vision of the Britain he wants to see a decade from now.

But there are already worries that this might become a fictional narrative unless he also focuses even more on the here and now.

After all, Sir Keir Starmer's "decade of national renewal" was binned after just two bumpy years in office.

Party insiders say measures such as removing VAT from electricity bills are just the start of that assistance.

But Labour's biggest union funder, Unite, wants to see much more robust action on living costs sooner rather than later. The union does not want the promise of jam tomorrow, but some instant sweeteners.

Its leader, Sharon Graham, has called for a "winter fuel in reverse" – a policy from Burnham next week which would be as popular as Starmer's early removal of payments from many pensioners was unpopular.

The union has put forward a motion which gives the PM plenty of options such as a cap on energy prices and unfreezing tax thresholds – an issue Burnham himself said had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to be the MP for Makerfield.

The union has said revenue can be raised through a windfall tax on banks. The umbrella body for unions, the TUC, has called for an increase in the bank surcharge to subsidise energy bills.

All eyes will be on John Healey's first conference speech as chancellor on Monday.

With borrowing costs for last month soaring to their second highest level, his room for manoeuvre is limited and he will not scoop his own Budget next month by announcing what is in it.

But Labour activists will be keen to know from his language whether Healey's Treasury will opt for continuity or will represent a break from the past two years under Rachel Reeves, not just in rhetoric but reality.

Some in Labour's ranks believe Burnham is planning for an early election, with party HQ recently launching "operation second term", to beef up its campaigning and organising strength.

Burnham does not have to call an election until August 2029 - but going to the country early - perhaps as early as next spring - could deliver him a mandate of his own and free him from the constraints of Sir Keir Starmer's 2024 manifesto.

Recent polling has suggested that a "Burnham bounce" is real, though not dramatic.

The party has moved from just under 20% in the polls at the end of the Starmer era to around the mid-twenties now.

Ipsos puts its standing as high as 28%, external, while YouGov registers a more modest 23%, external.

Labour strategists will be pleased that Reform UK's share – 21% in YouGov - is the lowest since January 2025, and that Nigel Farage's party is now neck-and-neck with Kemi Badenoch's Conservatives.

One Labour insider told me that Burnham is happy to see a resilient Badenoch, as this blunts Reform support and could point to a split vote on the right at an election.

And new research from YouGov, external suggests that at the all important constituency level, 63-68% of Lib Dem and Green voters would tactically vote for Labour to stop Reform UK winning their seat.

Burnham of course also faces a challenge on the left.

How much of a threat Zack Polanski's Greens can be in some traditional Labour seats will be tested in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election just a week after the Labour conference concludes.

Downing Street insists that an early election is not being planned.

To say anything else, though, would be to repeat the uncertainty of Gordon Brown's early months in No 10 when election speculation wasn't doused - and had become so rife that he was reputationally damaged when he decided not to go to the polls.

But some who have been in regular touch with No 10 tell me they have seen no serious signs that an early election is in the offing.

Burnham appears determined to give his government enough time in office to present tangible achievements to a sceptical electorate.

And with Labour still well below the 34% vote share it captured in 2024, many Labour MPs will be pushing the PM not to cut and run.

So don't expect the centre point of Burnham's conference speech to be a message to his MPs to go back to their constituencies and prepare for a loss of some of their seats.

But equally don't expect election speculation to subside at this conference.

The Labour Party has tried and trusted methods of managing dissent at party conferences, when it comes to votes on party policy.

But the coming week could see a concerted effort by some on the left to push for a complete ban on arms sales to Israel and for Israel's actions in Gaza to be described by Labour as a genocide.

Those close to Burnham believe he has gained considerable credit by sanctioning the illegal Israeli settlements on the West Bank and won't need to go further.

There is also some frustration that his government has not yet revised proposals to make migrants wait much longer to gain permanent residency rights, and there are genuine differences over whether the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields should go ahead.

But while Burnham is facing some difficult calls, this is not a leader facing a restless party in revolt.

He has offered to give the hard-pressed public "breathing space" amid a cost of living crisis.

And his own party is so far giving him breathing space as leader – largely sighing with relief that it is not Sir Keir Starmer who will be delivering the main address this year.

Senior Labour officials have hailed the forthcoming conference as an opportunity to "show voters a party that is boldly, confidently, and authentically Labour".

But not too far below the political radar, there are already demands from some in the wider Labour movement to prove it.

articles.title: UK summer 2026: BBC postcode lookup shows how hot and dry it was
articles.text:
Where does the data come from?

This lookup uses data from the HadUK Grid dataset (opens in new tab), which is produced by the Met Office Hadley Centre. HadUK Grid is one of the main products used by scientists to monitor and research the UK’s changing climate.

The data for 2026 is provisional, with fewer observations feeding into calculations due to lags in data availability. As such, the precise values could change slightly in future as more data comes available. The historical averages are calculated over a 30-year period from 1991-2020, which matches the standard period used by the UN’s World Meteorological Organization.

The HadUK dataset displays temperature and rainfall data across a uniform grid covering the entire landmass of the UK. The data does not cover the Channel Islands. Every value on the grid is an estimate for the centre point of a 1km by 1km grid box, the most detailed climate data publicly available for the UK. The values are created using observations from land-based weather stations across the country, and by taking into account additional factors such as altitude, terrain and distance from the coast to scientifically “fill in the gaps” between weather stations.

What do we mean by your area?

We’ve matched every active postcode in the UK to its nearest 1km by 1km grid cell in the HadUK dataset.

The results displayed for your area represent a mean average of that grid cell and the surrounding grid cells to your location. For most areas, this represents a 5km square centred on your postcode. Along irregular coastlines and on small islands, the nearest grid cells are chosen to match the shape of the coastline or island, but no cells are further than 7km away.

This approach aims to avoid sharp jumps between neighbouring locations which may occasionally arise due to uncertainties in the data, while still making use of the most detailed dataset available to capture local weather conditions across the UK's varied geography.

What does your area’s weather data represent?

The average temperature represents the mean average of the selection of grid cells across the month or season.

The maximum temperature is the mean average of the daily maximums recorded across all nearest grid cells for the month or season; the minimum temperature is the mean average of the daily minimums.

The rainfall is the total amount of rain for the month or season, averaged across the selection of grid cells.

To calculate the number of days above the heatwave threshold, we first averaged the daily maximum temperature for each grid cell with its nearest grid cells on every day. Using the Met Office’s heatwave thresholds (opens in new tab), we determined how many maximum daily temperatures exceeded the threshold for your location, based on the centre of your grid cell. Your area’s heatwave threshold may be approximate if your postcode is near a county boundary.

This is not the same as the number of days spent in an official heatwave, where the threshold has to be met or exceeded for at least three consecutive days.

Methodology support from Dan Hollis, Amy Doherty and Oli Claydon, UK Met Office.

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands expected in Paris for Pope Leo's visit
articles.text:
Pope Leo XIV embarks on a four-day visit to France on Friday, with the highpoint being a giant Mass attended by more than half a million people in central Paris.

For Saturday's afternoon celebration, an altar has been built on the Place de la Concorde and a large area around the Champs-Élysées sealed off by police.

Some 600,000 Catholic faithful are expected to cram the avenue up to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond.

Large crowds are also due at other stages in the Pope's itinerary, reflecting an enthusiasm that the Church attributes to growing spiritual thirst among the French and other Europeans.

President Emmanuel Macron will greet the Pope at Orly airport on Friday morning, and then hold talks with him at the Élysée Palace on geopolitical issues and artificial intelligence (AI). He will also deliver a speech with the Pope in Metz.

However, the president will not be at any of the Pope's Masses, largely to avoid breaching France's strict separation of state and religion.

Instead, the Champs-Élysées Mass will be attended by his wife Brigitte and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. Several candidates for next year's presidential election are also due, including Marine Le Pen of the nationalist right, centrists Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, and conservative Bruno Retailleau.

There were reports of tensions between Macron and the Vatican team sent to make arrangements, with the president allegedly frustrated in his wish for a more ceremonial aspect to the visit.

This was dismissed this week by Élysée officials, who said it was customary to offer a visiting head of state – which the Pope is – a range of high-profile events, such as a cavalry escort down the Champs-Élysées. But they said it was never expected that the Pope would actually take the offer up.

They did confirm that Pope Leo turned down Macron's idea of a meeting with artisans who helped rebuild the fire-devastated Notre-Dame cathedral. This was because his agenda was too tight, they said.

After a Popemobile ride through crowds to Notre-Dame cathedral on Friday afternoon, Pope Leo XIV will be joined in the evening by 80,000 young people at the Stade de France in northern Paris.

On Sunday 150,000 have signed up to attend mass in the Pyrenean sanctuary of Lourdes.

On Monday the Pope will be in Metz, in northeast France, where he will pay tribute to Robert Schuman (1886-1963), a founding father of the European Union and a fervent Catholic who is today a candidate for beatification.

The Pope will also meet a group of migrants in Paris, and in Lourdes some victims of sexual abuse by members of the Catholic clergy.

Born in Chicago in 1955, Pope Leo XIV was originally called Robert Prevost – a French name.

In fact his paternal grandmother was born in Le Havre in Normandy in 1894. When she married in the US many years later she and her Italian husband took the name Prevost, which had been her mother's maiden-name.

France has a historically complex relationship with the Catholic Church of Rome. The country was long known as the "Eldest Daughter of the Church" because supposedly, but inaccurately, it was the first kingdom to convert to Christianity. Actually Armenia, Georgia and Ethiopia preceded it.

In the 14th Century the papacy came in exile to Avignon in southern France, and over following centuries French armies periodically intervened in Italian politics, where popes were secular rulers as well as heads of the Church.

Napoleon held two popes in captivity.

Recent popes have all come to France, most notably John-Paul II, who came several times between 1980 and 2004, and Pope Francis who came three times, but avoided Paris, going instead to Strasbourg, Marseilles and Corsica.

articles.title: Media outlets banned by Trump denied access to White House event despite judge's order
articles.text:
CNN and MS NOW reporters say they have been denied entry to cover a White House state dinner despite a judge ruling their access to the grounds must be restored.

A federal judge said in an overnight ruling that the White House ban on three outlets - CNN and MS NOW and Politico - was likely unconstitutional and that the administration must allow them access, for now. Trump barred them last week, accusing them of "fake news".

Journalists with the three outlets were allowed back in on Thursday morning.

Then in the evening, a CNN reporter and a producer and an MS NOW reporter said that they were denied entry to cover the guests arriving for a state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

The outlets said they had properly submitted their reporters names for credentials to cover the arrivals.

CNN said that about an hour before Xi was scheduled to arrive, the White House said it could cover the event only with a photojournalist and audio technician, but not a team that included a reporter and producer.

MS NOW White House reporter Laura Barron-Lopez said she was told by White House staff that she could not be let in, and to contact the White House communications director.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

A White House communications account posted on X that "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event, and every press call".

The incident was the latest in a series of events on Thursday surrounding the ban on some media outlets at the White House.

Despite the overnight ruling, CNN, Politico and MS NOW all reported being denied entry to the White House on Thursday morning, prompting a request for an emergency court hearing.

In response, the director of White House Operations said in a court filing that the press passes and confiscated badges had been restored by 09:45 local time.

Shortly afterwards, all three outlets said they were allowed back in.

However, networks including Fox News, NBC, CBS and ABC, which pulled out in solidarity, have yet to confirm they will resume broadcast coverage from the White House.

The chaotic standoff limited some TV coverage as Trump welcomed Xi to the White House ahead of a state dinner.

articles.title: Miliband tells Iran minister UK will not tolerate 'hostile activity' on British soil
articles.text:
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi that the UK will "not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil".

The ministers met face-to-face at the UN General Assembly in New York City.

The Foreign Office said Miliband spoke to his counterpart about "the UK's unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups in UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community", and discussed war in the Middle East and a British couple detained in Iran.

There was no immediate comment from Araghchi. The Islamic Republic News Agency reported the men met and "discussed bilateral ties and international developments during their talks".

Miliband's comments follow an arson attack on four Jewish community ambulances in Golders Green in March and other incidents.

The BBC understands that British intelligence chiefs were initially keeping an open mind as to whether the Iranian state or organisations working for it had a role in the Hatzola ambulance attack and other attacks against Jewish communities during 2026.

They later concluded that secret intelligence pointed to Iran or its proxies being involved in the attack.

In July, a small power plant in the UK was also shut down due to a cyber attack, which the Telegraph reported , externalwas carried out by hackers affiliated to the Iranian regime.

The Foreign Office said Miliband also spoke to his counterpart about the country's war with the US, telling Araghchi that Iran should choose "de-escalation and diplomacy instead of prolonging the war" and stressing the importance of reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

In February, the US and Israel attacked Iran, killing the country's supreme leader.

Iran responded by launching strikes on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases. It also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, impacting the global economy.

On Wednesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the UN General Assembly that any deal would have to include an end to the US blockade stopping Iranian ships from using the waterway.

Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal is not reached soon, Pezeshkian said his country will never "bend the knee".

"The resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying," he said.

There was no immediate comment from the US, whose delegation walked out of the chamber at the start of Pezeshkian's address.

The Foreign Office said Miliband also used Thursday's meeting to raise the detention of British couple Lindsay and Craig Foreman in Iran.

The couple, who are from East Sussex, have been detained for more than 20 months after being arrested while passing through the country on a motorcycle journey.

In February, the Foremans were each sentenced to 10 years in jail on espionage charges, which they deny.

In Miliband's discussion with the Iranian foreign minister, he reiterated the call for them to be immediately released and stressed that their welfare remains a priority for the government, the Foreign Office said.

articles.title: 'It has broken us as a family,' mother of poison seller victim tells hearing
articles.text:
The mother of a British victim of poison seller Kenneth Law has said his death and the way that he died had "destroyed" their family.

Tanya Whitaker broke down at the start of her video statement about the death of her son, Samuel, shown on the second day of a four-day sentencing hearing of Law in Ontario, saying: "He barely had a chance."

The University of Warwick student was found collapsed outside his halls after taking poison sold by Law, who has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicide in Canada. British authorities have confirmed 79 UK victims also died after using his products.

Debbie Cornish echoed Whitaker's sentiments, telling the hearing that her family was "still fighting" to stay together years on from her daughter Danielle's death.

A plea deal with Canadian authorities means Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths, but impact statements from their families are being read this week.

"The enormity of losing a child is catastrophic," Whitaker told a Canadian court on Thursday. "Samuel was just 19 when he was handed the tools that ended his precious life."

She continued: "It has broken me completely and utterly. It has broken us as a family and me as a mother.

"Our son died alone at university 100 miles away from his family. We will never be able to forgive ourselves for this happening."

Whitaker said Samuel had been the only biological son of her husband, Paul.

"He is a shell of himself today. Broken and devastated beyond repair," she added.

Cornish, the mother of British victim Danielle, spoke of her anguish in a written statement, in which she referred to Law only by the initials KL.

"Words on paper can't even begin to describe the painful loss of our amazing daughter," she said.

"Nothing will be the same ever again as we are part of a surreal nightmare.

"Nearly four years on, we are still fighting to keep our family together... not to mention the constant thoughts of how she may have died.

"KL has changed the life of many many families all across the world as well as ours. We are living a constant nightmare."

Authorities say Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients from 40 different countries he met in online suicide forums. Roughly a quarter of the packages were sent to the UK.

He was arrested in May 2023, following a complex investigation by at least 11 law-enforcement agencies that involved investigators from around a dozen countries, including the UK, Italy and the US.

Aimee Louise Elif Walton, from Southampton, died in "the company of a stranger [she] met online", her sister told the court.

Adele Zeynep Walton said in a video played at the hearing that someone from a suicide forum had flown from the US and stayed with her in a hotel room for the 11 days leading up to her death.

"She died in a strange place, in a strange city, in the company of a stranger," her sister said.

"You only need to listen to the recording of the emergency call to know how much she suffered during the last moments of her life."

On Wednesday, the court heard from a British survivor who was given an antidote that saved her after taking poison from Law.

Elisabeth Belien told the court: "I feel guilty for surviving. Although I survived, it has also impacted my loved ones. I feel like my vulnerability was exploited. I still feel a lot of shame about what happened."

The hearing continues.

articles.title: Rapper Macklemore announces 'Free Palestine' tour after Ed Sheeran fallout
articles.text:
Rapper Macklemore is launching a "Free Palestine" tour, days after being dropped from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour following pro-Palestinian comments he made onstage earlier this month.

"So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit," he said upon announcing the tour on Thursday.

The American artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - said proceeds from the tour, which launches in Dublin next month, will go to organisations supporting Palestinians.

Macklemore's onstage comments and subsequent removal from the tour led Sheeran's support acts to drop out, while the British singer stressed that the decision to drop the rapper was made by his promoter, not by himself.

In a statement on Thursday, the rapper said that the last couple of weeks had shown him there had been "a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now".

"What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage," he said. "When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention."

Macklemore said he had spent the last week contacting artists who had used their platforms to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people, regardless of the consequences.

Due to how quickly the tour came together, several details were still being worked out, he added: "But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done."

Macklemore's new tour will begin in Dublin on 26 October followed by Paris on 29 October and London on 30 October.

US dates will also be added, he said, with additional tickets going on sale next week.

While performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in early September in New Jersey, Macklemore said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."

The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University.

After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out. He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza.

articles.title: Xi visit to Washington all pomp but little progress so far
articles.text:
At least so far, Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington has been all pomp and little obvious progress on pressing issues.

From the ceremonial welcoming at a military air base on Wednesday to the honour-guard arrival at the White House this morning, President Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet – literally and figuratively – for his Chinese counterpart.

The public remarks from the two leaders have teemed with warm words and diplomatic niceties. In a statement before today's formal meetings, Xi announced a gift of Chinese pandas and unveiled a new student exchange programme.

"Let us keep advancing the cause of friendship between our two peoples and work together to build a better world," he said.

Trump, for his part, outlined some of the topics the leaders planned to discuss in their meetings, including "pressing issues concerning security, technology, and superintelligence" - using his preferred term for artificial intelligence.

"The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come," he said.

The marching bands and military flyovers on Thursday may serve a larger purpose, however – at least for Trump.

"This is a little bit of intentional pageantry to talk up the positive vibes of the summit," Jennifer Welch, chief economic analyst for Bloomberg Economics, told the BBC. "This is very much how President Trump sees the summit and the role he plays in the US-China relationship, as ballast to provide stability."

Even so, there is still an edge to some of Xi's rhetoric, she notes.

In remarks at the White House, the Chinese leader again mentioned the "Thucydides trap" – a theory that shifts in global power tend to lead to conflict between rising and declining nations.

"China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust," Xi said.

The obstacles in the way of reaching any substantive agreement between the two nations are significant, however. When Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May, the men agreed to form boards of trade and investment to oversee economic interactions, and little more.

On Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a year-long trade "truce" between the two nations that had kept tariffs lower would be extended another two months. Financial analysts expect a further extension could come before this week's summit ends, given that neither side wants a renewal of last year's trade war.

The outlook for progress is much dimmer on other topics, like the US war with Iran, the Ukraine war and regulating AI.

China's reneging on promises to buy more American agricultural products and to also sell more rare earth minerals to the US is helping cloud the outlook. China, meanwhile, is watching to see if Trump follows through on a proposed sale of American weapons to Taiwan, which has been on hold for months.

articles.title: Four civilians killed in Pakistani strikes in Afghanistan, Taliban says
articles.text:
Afghanistan's Taliban government said a wave of Pakistani air strikes had killed four civilians in the latest escalation between the two sides.

The strikes hit provinces including Kandahar, the Taliban's base of power, sources told the BBC. A resident told AFP news agency they heard a jet, followed by a large explosion and then a fire in the city.

Pakistan said its forces had struck 10 targets in Afghanistan, without specifying their locations, adding the strikes were "strictly limited to identified military objectives".

It's the second wave of Pakistani air strikes on Afghan territory in the past week, and comes after a deadly attack on a police facility in Pakistan on 18 September.

In a statement, the Taliban said there would be an "appropriate response" following the attack, while Pakistan said any further "provocative act" would be responded to.

Taliban government spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said the attacks were in Afghanistan's Kandahar, Paktia and Khost provinces.

In Paktia, an official said jets had bombed the Afghan Armed Forces' 203 Mansouri Corps, which is controlled by the Taliban, without providing any information on casualties.

In Khost, a spokesman said houses were damaged in the strikes, with no casualties reported. Abdullah, a local eyewitness, told Reuters news agency the strikes happened around midnight.

"People were shouting, and there was panic all around," he said. "Afterwards, the village elder arrived and called out to the houses, asking if anyone was killed. Thankfully, no one was killed."

Another local, Salamat Khan, told Reuters that "there is no military base here, nor are there any military personnel", adding "there are only the homes of ordinary civilians".

Then on Wednesday, Pakistan said it detected drones launched from Afghanistan into its territory and that all of them were "neutralised". Taliban officials denied that their government had launched drones against Pakistan that day.

Unama said in July that cross-border armed violence between Taliban government forces and Pakistani security forces killed at least 499 civilians and wounded 1,216 others between October 2025 and June 2026.

The worst single incident occurred in March, when more than 269 people were killed, external in a Pakistani air strike on Kabul, which the Afghan Taliban said hit a drug rehabilitation centre. Islamabad denied the charge, saying it "precisely targeted military installations and terrorist support infrastructure".

The neighbouring countries had agreed a ceasefire in March, but international mediation has failed to produce a lasting resolution.

During a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly earlier this week, Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called for "concrete and verifiable" measures to ensure that Afghan territory is not used for "terrorism".

articles.title: Priest killed and four injured in knife attack at Polish abbey
articles.text:
A priest has been killed and four other people injured in a knife attack in south-east Poland, officials have said.

A 31-year-old Ukrainian man was arrested after the stabbings on the grounds of a Catholic abbey in the town of Jarosław.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki said Thursday's attack "has shaken us all and demands a firm response from the state", while his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky said "we are shocked by this evil".

Reports in Polish media said the attacker first injured a priest in a nearby cafe, and then another four people inside the abbey itself. A police investigation into the attacker's motives is now under way.

Polish police said four men and one woman were stabbed in the attack on Thursday morning on the abbey grounds.

The name of the murdered priest has not been publicly released.

Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said psychological support was now being provided to all those affected by the incident.

Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the perpetrator "will be punished with the full severity of Polish law".

Echoing his words, President Zelensky said "the perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility according to the law", adding that Ukraine was counting on "a quick and thorough investigation of all circumstances".

The Ukrainian embassy in Poland also condemned the attack.

In a statement, it said: "In such difficult moments, it is especially important to support each other, remain steadfast in respect for human life, and not allow pain to escalate into hatred or new violence. Responsibility for a crime must be based solely on the law."

Poland has recently seen a number of often violent incidents involving its citizens and Ukrainians, many of whom have fled their home country after Russia's full-scale invasion.

articles.title: 'We're all broke': Would you chase a friend for £5?
articles.text:
You pick up the bill for dinner, pay for the taxi home or grab a friend's coffee with the promise they'll pay you back later, but days go by and the money never arrives.

At what point do you ask them for it again and how small is too small to chase?

For some, $5 (£3.70) is worth a reminder, while for others, asking a friend to repay anything under $20 (£15) feels more awkward than simply taking the hit.

Henry Payne says he's "sent a request for $8.50, but I wouldn't go lower than $8".

The 21-year-old New Yorker adds that he will chase someone once but "two requests is insane".

"I would rather swallow the $8.50 than send another request."

He does admit that he's sometimes the person on the other side of the transaction and can be forgetful himself.

"For everyone that I haven't sent back money to, I just forgot, feel free to double request me."

Kaz Jahanbini, 19, says needing to ask to be paid back in the first place can be frustrating.

"If someone bought me something, I'm immediately paying them back. So then I'm thinking for them, what's the delay?"

His rule for navigating friendship and finances is to "keep your wallet close but your friends closer".

His friend Nouria agrees and says as a student "every extra dollar counts" but she would usually only ask for money back from a friend if it was more than $10.

A recent study, external found that 76% of Gen Z who have fronted money for a group expense, like a trip or event, say they were not fully repaid, and 55% say it created tension or negatively affected a relationship.

For British student Betsie Brooke-Taylor, 19, the threshold to ask for money back is a fiver as she says "every little helps".

She sees a cultural difference between the UK and US and even though "we are all broke, I think Americans are a bit more generous".

Betsie also thinks technology makes settling small debts easier in the US, where payment apps such as Venmo are widely used.

Venmo lets users send and request money through an app which includes the function of sending a reminder if someone hasn't paid you. In the US, more than 95 million people have a Venmo account, external.

"In the UK you have to ask for the account number and sort code, and not everyone has that on hand," she says.

For 19-year-old Annika Violet, the amount she would ask back from a friend depends on whether she's consistently paying for them.

"I prefer to do something where I get them this time and they get me next time but if I'm consistently paying and you're not, then I will request the $5."

Unlike many, Annika doesn't find money conversations uncomfortable.

"I am so confrontational, I do not find it awkward. If you're my friend, you would pay me back."

Annika's friend Hanako Stepper says she finds it awkward asking for money but wishes she didn't.

"I've never chased anyone - I'm just sad if I don't get paid back."

Annika's advice to those who do struggle to ask is to "be brave and bold".

"If they are going to give you flak about it, maybe it's a sign they are not a good friend."

Several people the BBC spoke to said the amount itself mattered less when somebody repeatedly failed to pay.

New York student Ella Feuille, 21, says $15 is roughly the point at which she would consider requesting money.

If a significant amount was owed, Ella says she would ask around three times before giving up but wouldn't necessarily forget about it.

"I have friends who I know now it has to go on their card because they're not going to pay me back."

Her friend Katrina Dimingot agrees and says she much prefers a method where "we don't pay each other back, we just take it in turns to get things for each other".
